issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: For a toxic chemical exposure trauma, water/flooding/large bodies of water is a poor fit as a trauma cue unless there is specific contamination-through-water context, which is not reflected anywhere else in the profile. The other items suggest generalized danger and intrusive memory, not a flood/water-based trauma context, so this trigger is hard to explain clinically.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships
issues.explanation: Avoiding new friendships or relationships is not well linked to the rest of the formulation. The profile centers on toxic exposure, hypervigilant threat monitoring, intrusive memories, and self-devaluation/hopelessness, but contains no interpersonal threat, mistrust, shame, or relationship-focused appraisals that would make this strategy a coherent consequence. It appears to target a symptom domain not otherwise represented in the selected items.

For toxic chemical exposure, hospital/antiseptic smell and darkness/nighttime can plausibly cue the event or its aftermath, but 'Known People: Related people' is hard to justify unless the trauma centrally involved family members. Nothing else in the profile suggests interpersonal betrayal, family-linked danger, or family members as part of the exposure, so this trigger appears poorly matched to the trauma type and the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
issues.explanation: The negative appraisals are heavily global and depressive/existential ('Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore', 'I have no future') rather than trauma-linked threat/self-appraisals. In this formulation Negative Appraisals has a very strong link to Threat, but the threat items are about persistent danger/vigilance in unfamiliar places. 'Can't rely on myself' fits that pattern; the meaninglessness/hopelessness items do not connect well to the toxic exposure theme, the selected triggers, or the specific threat content, making the node less coherent.

vignette:
Khanh was sixty-six years old, a roofer by trade, when the accident happened. On an unusually hot afternoon, a pressurized canister of industrial adhesive he was carrying across a hospital roof leaked directly into his face. Within seconds he could not breathe; his throat closed, his lungs burned, and he collapsed among the chemical stench. He spent the next ten days in the ICU, intubated and sedated, waking in the dark of the intensive care unit to the sharp antiseptic smell that clung to the curtains and his own skin. Those smells-the adhesive, the disinfectant, the faintly sweet odor of hospital soap-became seared into his memory, along with the suffocating panic of that first moment. Even now, months later, his memories of the event are not just clear and detailed but play over and over like a film he cannot stop, and sometimes the full emotional terror washes over him without any image at all, leaving him breathless. To stop the film from starting, Khanh began refusing any invitation that might take him somewhere new-social gatherings, family dinners at unfamiliar restaurants, even a short trip his wife suggested-so that the memories would have no new settings to latch onto, and before long his world had narrowed to the block around his house.

Since returning home, Khanh has found himself unable to relax even in his own living room, convinced that anywhere could be dangerous. The world, he now believes, is a fundamentally unsafe place. This belief makes him hyperaware of triggers: the moment darkness falls, or when he catches a whiff of antiseptic from a passing car, his concentration shatters and his muscles tighten. He avoids going anywhere unfamiliar because he cannot assess the danger there, sticking to the same grocery store and the same route to his few remaining roofing jobs. But those very routes had become reminders themselves-every time he passed the same intersection where a hospital smelled drifted from a passing ambulance, or walked the same aisle where the bleach cleaner sat on a shelf, his own avoidance had marked each spot as a place where the trauma was still alive and could reach him. He has also stopped asserting himself-never disagreeing with his wife or neighbors-because he is certain he cannot rely on himself to handle conflict constructively, and any disagreement might spiral into something he cannot control. When a hospital-like smell appears unexpectedly, like the bleach a janitor uses in a lobby, Khanh tries hard not to think about the trauma, shoving the images aside, but that very suppression makes the memory rush back more vividly later. He finds himself dwelling on who he used to be before the accident-the easygoing, decisive man who climbed scaffolds without a second thought-and that dwelling only deepens his sense of hopelessness, a feeling that he has no future worth planning for.

The connections between these experiences are tight and self-reinforcing. The hospital smells and the darkness not only trigger his intrusive memories but also amplify his sense of threat, making it impossible to relax; in turn, that chronic threat state primes his memory to replay more intensely. His negative appraisals-that the world is dangerous, that he cannot trust himself-make him more sensitive to triggers like the antiseptic odor, so that a faint whiff now feels like immediate danger. And his maladaptive strategies, such as avoiding assertiveness and suppressing thoughts, paradoxically increase his threat level; by never testing his ability to handle small conflicts, he remains convinced he is helpless, and the unprocessed memories stay raw. Trying not to think about the trauma actually brings the film-like replay to the forefront more often, and each time it does, his belief that he has no future tightens further.

At work, Khanh only accepts jobs on low, familiar roofs, and he refuses any site near a hospital or chemical storage. He has lost several contracts because of this, and his wife has started doing the shopping alone to spare him the distress of passing the pharmacy aisle. What finally brought him to seek help was a night last week when he woke at 3 a.m. in the dark, smelled the adhesive phantom-clear in his nose, and felt such a surge of panic that he could not get his breath back for nearly an hour. He is most afraid that this will never stop-that the smells and the darkness will keep closing in until there is nothing left of the man he used to be.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that intrusive memories directly cause or influence maladaptive strategies such as avoidance or thought suppression.
No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies directly cause or influence the perception or occurrence of triggers.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: No paragraph conveys that intrusive memories directly cause or influence maladaptive strategies such as avoidance or thought suppression.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies directly cause or influence the perception or occurrence of triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
